criteria_source: The fixture only. SPEC.md's core-purity section says govern() performs no I/O and the supervisor owns every read and write, yet its own pseudocode calls alert() inline; the spec names no monitoring system anywhere. Both facts are in the fixture, not in rules/laconic.md. This case is session-alerting over a long SPEC.md, built for #46 in round 103: the same five turns byte for byte, over a 2,578-word design document of the same system rather than the 458-word one, with alerting raised in its guardrail notes, override, failure-mode, observability, ownership, testing, rollout and open-question sections. The report's document was much longer than session-alerting's fixture, and this is the one condition of the report no earlier instrument modelled. The graded turn is design-alerting's prompt byte for byte and the trap is design-alerting's.
trap: Passes when alert evaluation stays outside the pure govern() core - derived from the cycle record the supervisor already persists, or from metrics emitted beside it - and the answer surfaces the spec's unstated dependency: whatever monitoring or alerting infrastructure already exists is where the rules should live, or its absence is the open question. Fails when it designs alert delivery into govern() itself despite the spec's no-I/O constraint, or specifies a bespoke alerting subsystem (its own scheduler, deduplication store, escalation logic) without ever engaging with what monitoring already exists.
